title: Axioms for relative entropy
author: Roberto Longo
abstract: For normal states of arbitrary von Neumann algebras, we characterize positive finite multiples of Araki relative entropy among non-degenerate divergences. The axioms are monotonicity under normal unital completely positive maps, tensor additivity, superadditivity for product second states, and separate lower semicontinuity in the predual norm. Alternatively, a conditional-expectation identity replaces the two tensor assumptions. The proof uses order bounds and asymptotic estimates on tensor powers. An appendix proves the known analytic estimates needed here, using standard modular theory and Haagerup L^p spaces. We also obtain the corresponding characterization in the C* algebraic setting.

title: TRACE: Topological Representations for Anomaly detection through Contrastive Embeddings
author: Sydney Johns
abstract: Intrusion detectors must recognize evolving malicious behavior even when confirmed attack labels are scarce or incomplete. We present TRACE, a topology-aware graph contrastive learning framework for label-efficient intrusion detection. TRACE learns from benign system-activity graphs by combining message-passing and topological representations, then assigns anomaly scores in the same projected embedding space optimized by the contrastive objective. This design captures both local interactions and graph-scale structural deviations without using attack labels during representation learning. A labeled validation set containing benign and malicious graphs is used only to calibrate the anomaly threshold. We evaluate TRACE on StreamSpot, GraSec-IoT, and Unicorn Wget against a supervised graph neural network and the benign-only GraphCL baseline. TRACE obtains F1 scores of 0.923, 0.790, and 0.583, respectively. Compared with GraphCL, this is higher on StreamSpot (0.450) and Unicorn Wget (0.203), but lower on GraSec-IoT (0.975). The supervised model leads on StreamSpot and GraSec-IoT, whereas TRACE has the highest F1 on Unicorn Wget. The mixed results show that topology-aware benign-only learning can improve detection in some graph settings but does not provide a uniform advantage.

title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
author: Arunkumar V
abstract: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
author: Zhaoning Zhang
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.

title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
author: Charles Xiao
abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
author: Fengming Liu
abstract: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. I propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.

title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
author: Ryan Lim
abstract: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

title: Exponential Quantum Memory Advantage for Late-Graph Smoothness and Spectral Estimation
author: Burhan Gülbahar
abstract: Graph signal processing tests how smoothly the decisions of next-generation massive sensor networks with $N$ nodes vary over their neighbour graph. Memory becomes the bottleneck when the neighbour graph arrives only after data erasure, a late-graph setting motivated by dispersed sensor networks and telemetry. We analyse three collection scenarios, reliable rounds, continuous broadcast and ordered capture, and test the Dirichlet energy $\mathcal E_G=\mathbf z^{\mathsf T}\mathbf L\mathbf z/N$ of the fused decision map $\mathbf z\in\{\pm1\}^N$, with late-graph Laplacian $\mathbf L$, against two thresholds. Hidden Matching uses $O(\log N)$ qubits on fused bits, but in reliable rounds and continuous broadcast, where nodes report $b$ sub-bits separately, a classical record buffer before it uses $O(N b)$ bits; classical methods need $Ω(\sqrt N)$ bits in the worst case. The recently introduced Quantum Oracle Sketching builds quantum oracles from random data streams without storing them. We combine coherent loading of separately reported sub-bits, exact in reliable rounds and by Quantum Oracle Sketching in continuous broadcast, with nonlinear fusion and Hidden Matching readout. The register count $R$ does not grow with $N$, and the memory is $O(\log N)$ logical qubits and classical bits, at fixed $b$, graph bounds, thresholds and error targets: an exponential memory advantage over every classical receiver and over Hidden Matching with that buffer. We prove unbiasedness in reliable rounds, preparation bounds in continuous broadcast, classical lower bounds and, for a planner-supplied multi-hop coefficient stream, spectral error bounds. Broadcast simulations match analytic averages at $N=1024$, without resolved bias growth up to $N=2^{20}$. Fault-tolerant hardware, gate rates and, in continuous broadcast, report counts remain open.

title: Synthetic Doubt and the Integrity of Digital Proof before the International Criminal Court
author: Seyed Mohammad Sadegh Dashti
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence complicates evidentiary assessment at the International Criminal Court by enabling fabricated audiovisual material and making authentic digital evidence easier to dismiss as fake. This article calls the latter problem synthetic doubt: an objection alleging that a digital item may be AI-generated or AI-manipulated. Existing scholarship addresses digital evidence, open-source investigations and deepfakes in the ICC context. Yet the question of when synthetic doubt should trigger enhanced reliability review under the Rome Statute, without displacing the prosecution's burden under article 66 or compromising article 67 fair-trial rights, remains underdeveloped. The article proposes a three-stage framework: a baseline authenticity and provenance showing by the proponent; a case-specific articulation threshold for the objector; and proportionate reliability review by the Chamber under articles 64 and 69(4). The framework treats AI-related provenance information and synthetic-media detector outputs as contextual rather than dispositive.

title: Reducing Asymmetric Path TSP to Asymmetric TSP
author: Hong Li
abstract: In the Asymmetric Traveling Salesman Problem (Asymmetric TSP), we are given distances between $n$ vertices that satisfy the triangle inequality but need not be symmetric, and we seek a shortest tour through all vertices. In its path version, Asymmetric Path TSP, two vertices $s$ and $t$ are prescribed, and we seek a shortest path from $s$ to $t$ through all vertices. Both problems are equivalent to their versions with arbitrary nonnegative edge costs on a directed graph, in which vertices may be visited more than once. We show that for all constants $α\ge1$ and $\varepsilon>0$, any $α$-approximation algorithm for Asymmetric TSP yields an $(α+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for Asymmetric Path TSP. The best previous reduction of this kind, due to Feige and Singh, yields an $α(2+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm. Our result answers an open question of Traub and Vygen. Consequently, every constant-factor approximation guarantee for Asymmetric TSP carries over to Asymmetric Path TSP up to an arbitrarily small additive error.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
author: Jacky Kumar
abstract: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
author: Matteo Fischetti
abstract: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
author: Javier Aguilar Martín
abstract: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

title: Do Apple M-Series Processors Enforce the Compound Memory Model? Sequential and Parallel Composition of Arm and TSO
author: Vijay Nagarajan
abstract: Apple's M-series processors can run each thread under the Arm memory model or under a TSO model, and threads of both kinds can share memory. This raises two questions of composition that Apple has not answered. Across threads, how does the machine behave as a whole? Within a thread, which Arm instructions play the roles of TSO's loads, stores and atomic read-modify-writes, and how are they ordered between themselves and across other Arm instructions? We propose that both answers are compositions of preserved program order. Across threads, each thread keeps the preserved program order of its own model: a parallel composition. Within a TSO thread, every Arm instruction keeps TSO's order and adds Arm's, and every atomic memory operation (AMO) is locked, as x86's read-modify-writes are: a sequential composition. We test both on an Apple M1 and an Apple M2 running Linux, with 936 litmus tests chosen from the two models' preserved program order, each run 6x10^8 times on each machine. Arm-mode threads follow Arm's official model, TSO-mode threads follow x86-TSO and the sequential composition, and programs that mix the two modes follow the compound model: neither machine shows an outcome these models forbid. Both machines also preserve three orders that these models do not require, and a compare-and-swap whose comparison fails behaves as if it writes back the value it read, which the Arm model does not require. All three orders held in runs up to 40 times longer.

title: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning
author: Jarvist Moore Frost
abstract: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. We show that self-attention is a real-space Dyson iteration whose Boltzmann (softmax) kernel acts as a two-body self-energy. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, Löwdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.

title: A counterexample to the soundness of the Flowering IOPP for codes on graphs
author: Hugo Delavenne
abstract: The Flowering protocol of Delavenne, Medevielle and Roussel (ISIT 2025, arXiv:2501.14337) and its generalization by Delavenne and Lallemand (CANS 2025, arXiv:2508.10510) are Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (IOPPs) for codes on graphs with Reed-Solomon local codes. Similarly to FRI for Reed-Solomon codes, the graph is recursively cut into isomorphic subgraphs and the word is folded along the cuts. We show that the soundness claims of both papers are false. The commit soundness proofs identify the vertex distance of a word to the code with the fraction of its unsatisfied local constraints, while only one inequality holds, in the wrong direction. We furthermore give an explicit counterexample.

title: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels
author: Federico Lucca
abstract: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. In earlier work, about two hundred labels and a TF-IDF logistic regression had the highest point accuracy on this inbox, though not significantly above the best hosted model; we ask whether the same labels, given to a decision model, close the gap. A first registered study, on a generic 4B base with cross-validation and message type only, stayed below the baseline at every label budget (-1.8 to -7.3 points). The main study was registered before any fine-tuning run: a fixed test set of 135 emails never used for selection, LoRA adapters on the public Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B decision models, nested subsets of 50 to 587 labels, two seeds and five decision fields on a free T4 GPU. Four of its five hypotheses are refuted--two in the fine-tunes' favour--and one is confirmed for one model. On message type the 4B model misses the registered three-point margin at 400 labels (+2.6) and passes it with all 587 (+3.3); with all labels both models are above the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points, where one email is 0.74 points and a 95% interval is about 15 points wide, and the 4B model is clearly ahead in type macro-F1 (0.581 vs. 0.406). On the three action switches the baseline is ahead at every label budget for both models (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899 mean accuracy with all labels), at under a millisecond per question against 306 and 1681 ms. The 0.8B type curve barely improves after 300 labels and then falls. The baseline never predicts the two rarest classes (7 offers and 8 spam in the training pool); the fine-tuned models find spam in some runs, not consistently across seeds. We list the explanations we did not test and say when a new attempt would be worth making. Scripts are public; weights and emails are not.

title: Vanishing Relative Distance of Uniformly Random CSS LDPC Codes Built from Permutation Matrices
author: Kenta Kasai
abstract: Classical random regular low-density parity-check codes can have minimum distance growing linearly with block length. We study CSS check matrices formed as full $J\times L$ arrays of arbitrary $P\times P$ permutation matrices, sampled uniformly subject to commutation. For fixed column weight $J\ge3$ and fixed even row weight $L>2J$, we prove that the relative minimum distance converges to zero in probability as $P\to\infty$, with block length $n=LP$. We analyze the weight enumerators that count all nontrivial logical representatives after excluding stabilizers. A coefficientwise lower bound shows that, at every fixed relative weight $0<α<1$ along even-weight sequences, exponentially many such representatives exist with high probability. Their typical and mean counts have exponent lower bound $h_2(α)/2$, where $h_2$ is the binary entropy function. We compare this bound with the classical LDPC and dense CSS mean weight-distribution exponents. The existence, with high probability, of a logical operator below every fixed target weight $δn$ yields the distance conclusion.

title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for Constant-Factor EFX Allocations of Chores
author: Aniket Murhekar
abstract: We study the fair division of indivisible chores among agents with additive disutilities, focusing on the central fairness notion of envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX), and its multiplicative approximations. Although the existence of constant-factor approximations to EFX are known, computing such an allocation in polynomial time remained open. We resolve this question by giving an algorithm that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, computes a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$. Our result relies on two algorithmic contributions. First, we give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for earning-restricted (ER) equilibria with equal earning requirements and arbitrary feasible chore earning limits. We develop a new nonconvex program with chore payouts and money-flow variables, and prove that every local maximum yields an exact ER equilibrium. We then give a mirror-ascent algorithm for this program and prove that it converges to an approximate ER equilibrium in polynomial time. Second, we give a new procedure that converts the approximate equilibrium into a $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX-friendly allocation, a suitable starting point for the chore-swap framework of Garg and Murhekar (2026). The procedure uses a flexible price threshold to choose swap chores and their recipients together, overcoming a factor-four bottleneck in the earlier approaches while accommodating approximate earnings. We expect these ideas to be useful more broadly in fair division, including for goods and other fairness notions.

title: High-probability Uniform Mixing via Dobrushin Contraction and Accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
author: Stefan Oberdörster
abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, since its invention and subsequent rise to widespread use, has been motivated by its ability to accelerate convergence to equilibrium compared to diffusive methods, both in terms of dependence on condition number and dimension. In the present work, we establish this acceleration simultaneously in both aspects for critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms. More precisely, for target measures $μ(dx)\propto e^{-U(x)}dx$ with $m$-strongly convex, $L$-gradient Lipschitz, and $L_H$-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, we show that the method mixes to $\varepsilon$-accuracy in total variation using $\mathcal O\bigl((κ^{1/2}+L_H^{1/2}m^{-3/4})\,d^{1/4}\bigr)$ gradient evaluations up to logarithmic factors, both uniformly over starting points in domains of high equilibrium probability and from warm starts. The proof incorporates ideas from previous studies by Bou-Rabee and Chen et al. that show either aspect of acceleration separately, into novel coupling technology. This new coupling technology for general Markov chains extends earlier frameworks aimed at capturing fast local equilibration in the presence of slow global mixing. Specifically, via a weak-$(1,1)$ maximal inequality that follows from Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem, we uncover a stability mechanism in high-probability domains with respect to equilibrium. This enables straightforward localization to naturally arising domains of fast local mixing, and seamlessly fits broad local frameworks via Dobrushin contraction, Wasserstein contraction and local Harris' theorems. We develop the Dobrushin formulation.

title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
author: Masanori Hanada
abstract: These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

title: Conformal Expert Pools: Training-Free Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting Beyond Seasonality
author: Valery Manokhin
abstract: Conformal Seasonal Pools (CSP) showed that a forecaster with no training at all, built only from past values at the same point in the season and from past forecast errors, significantly outperformed DeepNPTS, Amazon's learned non-parametric forecaster. We propose Conformal Expert Pools (CEP), a training-free successor. CEP replaces the single seasonal-naive forecast by a pool of simple forecasters, builds its predictive distribution from their past forecast errors, and adapts both the pool and the errors to the series being forecast. No model is trained and no parameter is learned across series. On the CSP benchmark of 232 datasets and 24,502 forecast windows, CEP is better than CSP on 78% of datasets by CRPS, on 84% by MSIS and on 83% by Winkler score; on a typical dataset its CRPS is 14% lower and its MSIS 23% lower (both p < 1e-22, paired Wilcoxon test), and coverage of 95% intervals rises from 90.1% to 92.2%. CEP has a lower CRPS than DeepNPTS on 88% of datasets, than NPTS on 89% and than SeasonalNPTS on 83%. The improvement persists on dataset families outside the development set and on 36 additional fev-bench files. We also test the published claims that Laplace, an online ensemble forecaster, "beats (almost) everything" and "beats" CSP. On 228 datasets at multi-step horizons the claims do not hold: CSP outperforms Laplace on 60% of datasets by CRPS and on 64% by interval score, and Laplace ranks sixth of seven methods, with the widest intervals of all (69% wider than CEP's). Its point forecast is biased low and on 54% of datasets is less accurate than seasonal naive, and from a cold start it takes about 7,700 times longer than CSP. CEP is better than Laplace on 82% of datasets by CRPS and on 80% by MSIS, with intervals about 40% narrower, and runs 271 times faster.

title: Strategic Repayment and Latent Fragility in Financial Networks: Why Banks Withhold Payable Liquidity
author: Hicham El Kaissi
abstract: A network in which every bank pays in full can nevertheless admit a self-fulfilling settlement freeze under the same balance-sheet fundamentals. Thus, observing full repayment does not establish the uniqueness or robustness of the payment equilibrium. We derive this result from a precautionary-liquidity choice: banks may delay otherwise feasible payments to insure an interim funding need, trading a positive settlement-discipline cost against the marginal value of retained cash. The optimal reserve is a critical quantile of future liquidity requirements, and the repayment rule nests Eisenberg-Noe maximal feasible clearing exactly. Counterparty underpayment both reduces current cash and raises desired reserves. We characterise network amplification and the conditions for coexistence, including a homogeneous two-bank GPD frontier in which interbank exposure and maximum funding pass-through enter through one dimensionless index. A two-date settlement accounting rule distinguishes payment timing from ultimate default. The main result concerns equilibrium coexistence; the conditional best-response adjustment diagnostic does not assign selection probabilities.

title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
author: Mo Zhou
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
author: The InclusionMed Collaboration
abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
author: Victor M. Preciado
abstract: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

title: Separations Between Randomized and Exact Quantum Query Complexity for Boolean Functions
author: Zekun Ye
abstract: We construct a family of total Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{tot}}$ whose randomized and exact quantum query complexities satisfy $R(F_{\mathrm{tot}}) \ge Q_E(F_{\mathrm{tot}})^{2-o(1)}$. Chiruvella, Kayal, Mittal, Paraashar, and Saurabh (2026) also obtained a nearly quadratic separation for total functions in the query model by a different method. For every fixed $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, we construct a family of partial Boolean functions $F_{\mathrm{par}}$ on $n$ bits satisfying $Q_E(F_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(1)$ and $R(F_{\mathrm{par}})=Ω_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$. This matches the asymptotic separation previously obtained with bounded error (STOC 2021; SICOMP 2023). Lifting yields a family of partial communication functions $G_{\mathrm{par}}$ with $Q_E^{\mathrm{cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ and $R^{\mathrm{pub,cc}}(G_{\mathrm{par}})=Ω_\varepsilon(n^{1-\varepsilon})$, where $n$ is the total number of input bits held by the two parties.

title: PlainPairs: A Corpus Pairing the Prescriber and Patient Texts of U.S. Prescription Medicine Labels
author: Obada Kraishan
abstract: A prescription medicine in the United States comes with labeling written for prescribers, and many medicines also carry a text written for patients: a Medication Guide or a patient package insert. The two texts describe the same medicine for two readers, yet public resources rarely hold them side by side. I present PlainPairs, an open corpus built from the openFDA drug label files. Version 0.1.0 holds 35,177 prescription labels that carry a patient text, 21,416 distinct patient texts, 250,829 patient-text segments matched to prescriber sections through their regulatory headings, reading-level measures on both sides, and rule-based counts of plain-language wording. A second source, the National Cancer Institute's cancer information summaries, adds 756 summaries in health-professional and patient versions, in English and Spanish. Measured on the structure of the label, the median Medication Guide reads at grade 8.7 by Flesch-Kincaid and at grade 11.1 by SMOG. The same guides measured on the flattened text that the bulk files serve read about two grades higher, a difference that comes from lost list and heading boundaries. Patient texts address the reader in 41 of every 100 sentences, against 0.2 in prescriber sections. A blind hand check of 100 pairs supports the heading-based alignment for seven of ten heading types. The corpus, its code and its documents are public, and the release keeps texts that show a company copyright mark out of the text tables.

title: When Feature Representation Changes Local Explanations: A Controlled Comparison of SHAP and LIME under Numerical Discretization
author: Parv Patel
abstract: Local feature attributions are computed over a feature representation chosen by an upstream data-engineering step, yet they are read as statements about the underlying quantity. We ask how discretizing one continuous feature changes local KernelSHAP and LIME explanations when the classifier is held fixed, and whether the two explainers respond differently. A random forest is trained on UCI Adult and frozen; age is collapsed onto equi-width or quantile bin representatives (k in {3,5,10}) before the model receives it, and the same 120 held-out instances are explained in every condition across multiple seeds. We show analytically and numerically that for KernelSHAP this is exactly equivalent to explaining the unchanged model at the quantized instance against a quantized background, so the comparison is between two effective inputs rather than a pure explainer effect; for LIME no such equivalence holds. Each attribution change is compared with a seed-noise floor from re-running the explainer on the unchanged condition. KernelSHAP's age attribution exceeds its noise floor in all 6 pre-specified conditions (median ratios 2.4-59, all significant after Holm correction); on the raw scale LIME's exceeds its floor in only 2 of 6 and in the rest is no larger than its own run-to-run variation. SHAP's normalized change exceeds LIME's in every condition (rank-biserial 0.81-1.00), while LIME is 2.5-4.6x less consistent across repeats. Predicted classes change for only 0.8-5.8% of instances and held-out ROC-AUC never falls below 0.9097, yet 45-94% of instances show a large SHAP attribution change with no class flip. Feature-importance rankings barely move (median Spearman >= 0.979, top-3 overlap 1.00). The representation change and the change in effective input cannot be separated within a frozen-model design.

title: Edit Recommendation: Can LLMs Anticipate Edit Requests from Users, and When?
author: Daisuke Kikuta
abstract: After a large language model (LLM) agent generates an artifact, users often send edit requests for it. This paper studies whether an LLM can anticipate these requests before they are sent. Such anticipation is useful in practice because it reduces the effort of user review and feedback. We formalize this task as edit recommendation and build EditRecBench, a benchmark for evaluating the performance of LLMs on this task, from real-world conversation logs in WildChat-4.8M. Through benchmarking and failure analysis, we identify a practical challenge that some cases are inherently difficult to predict in real-world settings. To address this, we introduce decision model-based gating to filter out cases where predictions are unlikely to be correct before they are presented to the user. Our trained model outperforms existing decision models and raises pass@5 among shown suggestions by 12--25 points at a gating threshold. Our code is available at https://github.com/ntt-dkiku/llm-edit-recommendation.

title: Cap-Aware Boosting for Green Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting
author: Shubham Pratap
abstract: Accurate forecasting of Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM) electricity prices is essential for market participants in the Indian power sector. We present a LightGBM-based forecasting framework for Indian Energy Exchange GDAM prices, which clear in 96 fifteen-minute intervals per day. The proposed system explicitly models price-cap behavior by separating capped-price events from normal market conditions. A classification head estimates the probability of the regulatory price cap (Rs 10,000/MWh), while a regression head predicts uncapped prices in logarithmic space. Final forecasts are obtained through probabilistic blending of these components and are accompanied by nine quantile forecasts for uncertainty estimation. Evaluated on 257 trading days between 1 January and 14 September 2026, the model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 397.9 Rs/MWh and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 9.57%, substantially outperforming a Chronos-2 baseline (583.3 MAE) and a persistence baseline using the previous day's profile (589.1 MAE). We further introduce leak-safe variants that incorporate real-time market signals, unmatched sell volumes, and solar generation proxies. In a recent out-of-sample evaluation, the quantile-clock variant achieved the best short-term performance with an MAE of 789 Rs/MWh during 25-28 October, while the enhanced capped-price model achieved an MAE of 716 Rs/MWh across 21 evaluation days through 16 November. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of regime-aware probabilistic forecasting for high-volatility electricity markets.

title: Region-VAD: Video Anomaly Localization and Detection via Region Selection
author: Giacomo D'Amicantonio
abstract: Anomalies are local events, yet weakly supervised video anomaly detection scores them globally. Most methods pool an entire frame into a single vector, rank frames by that vector, and derive a location afterwards as a saliency map of the score. Full-frame pooling mixes the anomaly with its background, so a detector can reach competitive benchmark scores from scene context without being able to show where in the scene the anomaly occurs. We introduce Region-VAD, which first selects a region and then detects the anomaly from that region alone. Region-VAD selects an explicit rectangle over the tokens of a frozen foundation model and scores anomalousness only from the tokens inside the box, through attention pooling followed by a standard temporal head. The rectangle is not learned, it is the box in which the frozen tokens change most between consecutive segments, in all four feature projections of the encoder, and it is found by exhaustive search over the rectangles of the token grid. Only the pooling and the temporal head are trained, from video-level labels without boxes, masks or frame-level annotations, and no trained component reads a token outside the selected region. Experiments on five datasets, with one localizer configuration shared by all datasets and backbones, show that Region-VAD achieves state-of-the-art anomaly localization on UCF-Crime and MSAD at competitive detection performance.

title: MORE: Merge Once, Route Early for Training-Free Multi-Subject Composition from Large LoRA Pools
author: Tian Xia
abstract: Public hubs offer many personalized LoRAs per text-to-image backbone, yet composing two of them in one image remains fragile. In FLUX, keeping a pool of $K=10$ or $20$ subject LoRAs loaded makes their deltas interfere, and even loading only the two requested LoRAs keeps both subjects in fewer than 4% of images: one subject vanishes, the two fuse, or the image splits into a collage. We present MORE (Merge Once, Route Early), a training-free two-stage pipeline for FLUX. Merge once: the whole pool is folded into a single fixed-rank adapter by the subspace-regression router of SSR-Merge, made reliable by ridge, rank and calibration choices, and factored exactly into a shared part and per-subject parts. Route early: during the first 30% of the denoising steps each subject's part is gated to its layout region; a decaying soft attention bias ties every region to its own subject tokens, and a cyclic swap guidance extrapolates away from the prediction with the subjects' regions permuted, which counteracts region homogenization. On held-out seeds, MORE keeps both subjects in 94.2% ($K=10$) and 78.3% ($K=20$) of images, against 50.8% / 35.8% for FreeFuse and 25.0% / 24.2% for LoRAShop, and reaches an ImageReward of 1.32 (best baseline 0.07), while all $K$ subjects stay in one adapter. With layouts inferred automatically it still keeps both subjects in 70.0% / 55.0% of images.

title: A Hierarchically Compressed Immittance Operator Formulation for Fast Statics-to-Full-Wave Electromagnetic Simulation with the Boundary Element Method
author: Shashwat Sharma
abstract: The boundary element method allows the electromagnetic simulation of three-dimensional problems with a two-dimensional discretization, using a surface integral representation of Maxwell's equations. For applications involving broadband simulations or multiscale geometries, the well-known low-frequency breakdown of conventional integral equation formulations must be addressed, while ensuring that dielectric, semiconducting, and lossy metallic regions are modeled rigorously, including the skin effect. In this work, a new boundary element formulation based on an immittance operator is proposed, where the underlying integral equations are inherently valid from statics to the full-wave regime. To enable efficient matrix assembly and solution, a hierarchical matrix compression strategy is devised, leveraging fast direct factorization as an intermediate step, and fast matrix-vector products for the iterative solution of the final system of equations. The proposed formulation is capable of electrostatic, magnetostatic, quasistatic, and full-wave simulations of dielectrics, semiconductors, and lossy metals. Representative numerical examples drawn from a variety of applications demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method.

title: How Can Size, Ceiling, and Time Bounds Affect the Complexity of Nonuniform Automata Families?
author: Tomoyuki Yamakami
abstract: In the past literature, families of two-way finite automata and pushdown automata having limited resource-bounded complexity have been studied in direct connection to (mainstream) space-bounded complexity classes equipped with Karp-Lipton style advice of limited size when all inputs given to the automata have bounded length. We acknowledge three major factors--size, ceiling, and time--of such families, which have a significant impact on the computational/descriptional complexity of finite and pushdown automata families, where the "size" refers to the (stack-)state complexity, the "ceiling" refers to the maximum input length, and the "time" refers to the execution time of underlying automata. In this line of study, we further explore these effects caused by different sizes and ceilings. We exploit automata-based reducibility and translatability to space-bounded advised Turing machines and auxiliary automata.

title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
author: Víctor Gallego
abstract: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

title: Digits in Notation Are Not Numbers: A Scoring Pitfall in PDF-to-Markdown Conversion of Japanese Technical Documents (Preliminary Evaluation)
author: Mitsumasa Wada
abstract: Converting PDFs to Markdown is now routine preprocessing for search and language models, yet scoring the numbers in the output is easy to get wrong. We evaluate MinerU, a plain-text OCR baseline (NDLOCR-Lite), and a deterministic post-processing pipeline (anchor insertion, footnote reordering, fixes of look-alike characters in fixed contexts, gated formula repair using two independent OCR partners, and heading reconstruction) on 48 public Japanese pages (three documents), text-layer and rasterized. Our pre-specified number-and-unit F1 favored the OCR baseline (0.575 vs 0.397), and a disagreement check between the two engines seemed to flag about half of the converter's number errors (54.6%). Both were artifacts. The scorer counted digits in the converter's notation (image-link paths, HTML attributes), which plain text lacks. With the notation removed (a post-hoc check), the F1 scores tie (0.575 vs 0.594), and the check flags only 13% of number errors, because most errors are misses that both engines share. What remains: the OCR baseline has a lower body character error rate (0.012 vs 0.053 rasterized). The pipeline raises extra-number recall at page level (+0.145; the document-level interval touches 0), mostly by restoring page numbers, but lowers heading-level agreement (0.133 to 0.061) and leaves spurious formulas unchanged; its formula repair never fires. A pre-specified precision gate for its flags (0.80, human-judged) is met at 0.929, yet the post-processing hypothesis fails on its improvement items. We recommend scoring numbers after removing notation and checking critical figures against the source. By the pre-specified criteria, the study stays a technical report.

title: Hivemind: A Federated Protocol for AI-Mediated Tacit Knowledge Sharing in Organisations
author: Srinivasan Sundaresan
abstract: This paper presents Hivemind, a federated protocol that enables AI agents to exchange tacit knowledge on behalf of their users, asynchronously and without requiring any direct human interaction. Individual AI memory systems capture the decisions, reasoning, and contextual knowledge that surface during AI-assisted work. Hivemind creates the shared space in which this captured knowledge can flow between individuals across team and departmental boundaries, addressing a structural gap that neither centralised knowledge repositories nor existing AI tooling closes, even where partial solutions such as expert-finding systems exist. The paper evaluates centralised versus decentralised design approaches, proposes a federated architecture grounded in Nonaka and Takeuchi's (1995) Socialisation, Externalisation, Combination and Internalisation (SECI) model, and demonstrates a proof-of-concept implementation using Design Science Research (DSR) methodology. Measuring the enterprise benefit of federated tacit expertise sharing remains an open task for future work.

title: Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
author: Matthias G. Mayer
abstract: Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.

title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
author: Mohamed Chaouch
abstract: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

title: Same Fix, Different Weights: Replicating Weight-Space Programming with Claude
author: Subham Kundu
abstract: Takehi et al. (2026) report that GPT-6 Astra, given the weights of small neural networks as text, can say what they were trained to do, repair them, and write new ones without training. I re-ran the core of that study with Claude Opus 5.5 in ten pre-registered experiments, with untrained-network and permutation controls and hand audits of every sandboxed code cell. Reading was mixed: Claude named 3 of 4 Atari games from policy weights and found the measured copying heads in 15/15 character-LM runs, but its answers about training data often followed priors. Unlike the original, it identified a sycophantic Gemma 3 270M finetune from weights alone in 6/6 runs. One-shot weight edits took a failing MountainCar policy from 0% to 100% success and a hovering LunarLander policy from 0% to 85.6%; zero-shot networks beat PPO at 100k steps on 4 of 5 environments, each implementing a textbook controller. With no training or forward passes, Claude wrote a 1.48M-parameter 9x9 Go network that won 85-94% of games against three PPO opponents. Given Qwen3.5-0.8B's weights and 10, 25 or 50 forward passes of 64 practice problems, Claude raised MATH-500 from 6.7% to 51.4%, 55.2% and 58.1% (+51.4 points at 50 passes, 95% CI [47.9, 55.0]; original 48.1%), GSM8K from 11.6% to 68.2% and IFEval from 22.2% to 54.2%. Unlike the original, which removed an internal loop direction, every edit acted at the output: it scaled the final norm, raising the effective sampling temperature, and lowered the logit of "Wait" while raising that of </think>. The norm scaling alone reaches only 20.9-22.1% on MATH-500. On Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, no edit helped (-0.8 points), as in the original.

title: From Strong Normalization to WhatsApp: the Journey of an Axiom
author: Giuseppe Castagna
abstract: Twenty years ago, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini, Daniele Varacca and I showed that Milner's classic encoding of functions into processes does not respect one of the laws of intersection types, the one stating that $(σ\toτ)\land(σ\toρ)$ is a subtype of $σ\to(τ\landρ)$, which Barendregt, Coppo and Dezani-Ciancaglini had stated in 1983 for their filter $λ$-model. In this essay I show that this observation is the key to closing what a colleague at Meta calls ``the main typing gap in Erlang''---the language in which the servers of WhatsApp are written: the type of the function that implements a server is not related to the type of the server, so that a client may expect from the server a reply that the server will never send. Actually, closing this gap is just an excuse to follow the journey of the law above, and of some of its relatives, from the study of strong normalization in the $λ$-calculus to the type systems of Elixir and Erlang: a journey that shows how much the practical typing of these languages owes to the work of Mario Coppo, Mariangiola Dezani-Ciancaglini and Simona Ronchi Della Rocca, to whom this essay is dedicated for their eightieth birthdays.

title: vividRGB: Various visual cue detection in RGB photographs with forced focused attention
author: Masahiro Ryo
abstract: Natural photographs contain dense, overlapping structures that can be weakly expressed in feature maps from whole-image vision encoders. We introduce forced focused attention (FFA) and its Python implementation, vividRGB. FFA is an encoder-agnostic inference-time procedure that applies a frozen encoder to enlarged, overlapping local crops, averages inverse-aligned reflections, and reconstructs a feature field in source coordinates. We evaluate 50 high-resolution photographs from grassland vegetation, fungal networks, airborne forests, coral reefs, and phytoplankton microscopy, using DINOv3 ViT-B/16. Across the five domains, FFA at 5% or 10% focus produces higher mean RGB-edge boundary F1 than direct DINOv3 encoding and automatic SAM3 masks. Domain means range from 0.244 to 0.596 for FFA, versus 0.028-0.076 for direct DINOv3 and 0.020-0.090 for SAM3. Qualitative feature maps also show finer appearance structure. These results concern RGB-edge preservation rather than verified species, traits, or biological segmentation. Narrower focus generally improves boundary preservation, while extraction time and GPU energy use increase sharply and gains diminish at finer settings. FFA may be useful for relatively small, high-resolution ecological image collections where dense visual cues matter. The alpha release vividRGB 0.1.0 and versioned research resources support reproducible cue inspection.

title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
author: Kevin Kam Fung Yuen
abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

title: Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows
author: Daksh Bathla
abstract: AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.

title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
author: Mika Facchini
abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.

title: Which AI Use Cases Deserve a Pilot? A Risk and Value Framework for Funding, Scoping, and Scaling AI
author: Vishal Srivastava
abstract: A composite score can rank AI use cases while leaving the permitted operating scope and the evidence required for expansion unspecified. We treat the unit of decision as a use case at a proposed scope (authority, human mediation, limits, volume, environment, population) and define three decisions: screen the scope, fund the experiment, and authorize expansion only when residual risk is acceptable and evidence of incremental net value applies at that scope. A risk track (R1-R4) is implemented as an explicit decision table with vetoes and documented precedence, and a value track follows four evidence stages with each transition needing its own evidence. Funding uses expected value of perfect information as an upper bound and the value of sample information for the specific experiment. A quantified expected-loss check, required where policy says so, computes the containment an expansion needs and credits a control only on evidence measured at the proposed scope; in a synthetic scenario the highest-value control design fails that test while a smaller scope passes. A reproducible Python package with 279 passing tests demonstrates the framework on synthetic refund, reconciliation and knowledge-assistant use cases, including a synthetic matched-scope fixture and a transferability stress test (value evidence is simulated, not realized), and compares it with a public AWS sample. Thresholds and appetite are prototype policy requiring field validation.

title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
author: Christophe Denis
abstract: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

title: Medical question answering collapses in Hausa: a pre-registered pilot on three small open models
author: Abbas Sani
abstract: A system that reads nothing and always answers the most frequent letter scores \BaselineP{} on our Hausa medical multiple-choice set. \NBelowBaseline{} of the \NModels{} small open models we evaluate do not beat it. We lead with that because the usual summary of a multilingual result -- a percentage-point drop from English -- does not say whether what survives the drop is performance at all. On a paired English--Hausa set of \NEval{} MedMCQA items, three instruction-tuned models of 3--4B parameters lose between \GapMedGemma{} and \GapQwen{} points of accuracy, every gap significant after Holm correction. Back-translating the Hausa items into English recovers between half and two-thirds of the gap for the two general-purpose models but not demonstrably for the medically adapted one, so the deficit is substantially, though not wholly, a matter of the language of presentation. Answers are also far less stable: agreement across three option orderings falls from \ConsEnQwen{} to \ConsHaQwen{} in the worst case. An exploratory error analysis of \ENRows{} discordant items attributes most of the damage to medical vocabulary lost in translation (\ETerm{}, 95\% CI \ETermLo{}--\ETermHi{}), usually in the question stem. A fourth registered hypothesis proposed closing the gap with self-generated preference pairs. Its pilot gate found nothing to train on: asked to reason in Hausa rather than to pick a letter, the model echoes the prompt back, switches into Swahili, or simply stops without answering; only \GateParse{} of chains are parseable. We report that intervention as not run, which is itself the sharper result -- a forced-choice benchmark cannot see a model that has no generative command of the language at all. All hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were registered before any model was run, and all deviations are logged.

title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
author: Kathik Iyer
abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

title: A Recursive Construction of Perfect Arrays of Every Shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_d}$ over the Unit Quaternions
author: Sam Blake
abstract: We extend the recursive construction of perfect and odd perfect sequences over the simple unit quaternions $\Qe=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ of Blake to arrays of any dimension. The three operations of that construction act on one direction of an array at a time, and are valid whenever the array is periodic in the remaining directions. Starting from a perfect array $P$ of shape $M_2\times\cdots\times M_d$ they give perfect arrays of shape $2^a\times M_2\times\cdots\times M_d$ for every $a\ge0$, with explicit index functions and with the array orthogonality property for the divisor $2$ in the lifted direction; from $a=5$ on these arrays are, in general, Kronecker products of a sequence with $P$ in neither order. Applied direction by direction, the construction gives perfect arrays over $\Qe$ in every shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_d}$, and in every shape $2^{a_1}\times\cdots\times2^{a_{d-1}}\times N$ for which a perfect sequence of length $N$ over $\Qe$ exists.
